claim: (b) Ecloga of Leo III and Constantine V, Title II: minimum ages (draft: 13 girls, 15 boys)
ref: Ecloga of Leo III and Constantine V (726), marriage-contract excerpt (Fordham page does not number the title; the 'Title II' label is from the assignment and is not confirmed by this source)
quote_orig: not obtained (Fordham page gives English only)
quote_en: "The marriage of Christians, man and woman, who have reached years of discretion, that is for a man at fifteen and for a woman at thirteen years of age, both being desirous and having obtained the consent of their parents, shall be contracted either by deed or by parol."
edition: Translation by E. H. Freshfield, A Manual of Roman Law: The Ecloga (Cambridge, 1926), pp. 72-74; reprinted in Geanakoplos, Byzantium (Chicago 1984), pp. 266-67, as reproduced on Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook (ed. Paul Halsall, 1997; page revised later). Fordham states: permission for electronic copying, educational and personal use; no commercial use. Freshfield 1926 public-domain status not checked.
what_it_says: The Ecloga sets the age of marriage at 15 for a man and 13 for a woman, with the proviso 'years of discretion'. The excerpt does not mention consummation or any consummation age.
limits: Secondary web reproduction of a 1926 translation; I read only this excerpt, not the Greek text. The excerpt is in a section on marriage contracts; it does not contain the sentence about consummation. The Greek was checked separately: see S3-11 (Lingenthal 1852 edition, Title II cap. 1: men from 15, women from 13).

claim: (a) Justinian Institutes 1.10 and Digest 23.2.4: minimum marriage ages (draft: 14 males / 12 females); and betrothal at seven
ref: Institutes of Justinian 1.10 pr. (Title X 'Of marriage'); Institutes 1.22 pr. (Title XXII 'Of the modes in which guardianship is terminated'; the passage on puberty of males and the age at which females are fit for marriage); Digest 23.2.4 (Pomponius, 3 ad Sabinum)
quote_orig: Dig. 23.2.4 (Pomponius 3 ad Sab.): "Minorem annis duodecim nuptam tunc legitimam uxorem fore, cum apud virum explesset duodecim annos."  Dig. 23.1.14 (Modestinus 4 diff.): "In sponsalibus contrahendis aetas contrahentium definita non est ut in matrimoniis ... id est, si non sint minores quam septem annis."
quote_en: Institutes 1.22 pr. (Sandars 1876, Title XXII): "Consequently by the promulgation of our sacred constitution we have enacted that puberty in males shall be considered to commence immediately on the completion of the fourteenth year, leaving unaltered the rule judiciously laid down by the ancients as to females, according to which they are held fit for marriage after completing their twelfth year."  Institutes 1.10 pr. (Sandars 1876): "Roman citizens are joined together in lawful wedlock when they are united according to law, the man having reached years of puberty, and the woman being of a marriageable age, whether they be independent or dependent."  Digest 23.2.4: no PD English opened (see own translation).
own_translation_en: Dig. 23.2.4: "A girl married while under twelve becomes a lawful wife only when, with her husband, she has completed twelve years." Dig. 23.1.14: "In contracting betrothals the age of the parties is not fixed as it is for marriages; so betrothals can be made even from the earliest age, provided it is understood that each party is not younger than seven years."  (my literal English, not a published translation)
edition: Sandars, The Institutes of Justinian (1876; Gutenberg ebook 5983, public domain). Digest: Latin from thelatinlibrary.com (Mommsen-Krueger text, public domain); no English translation was opened.
what_it_says: Justinian's Institutes (1.22 pr.) give puberty for men at 14 and say that, by the older rule, women are fit for marriage after 12. The Digest (Pomponius) makes a marriage with a girl under 12 a lawful marriage only once she has completed 12 years with her husband. Betrothals were not fixed by age as marriages were, but both parties had to be at least seven (Modestinus).
limits: Institutes 1.10 pr. gives no numerical age; the numbers 14/12 are in 1.22 pr. (end of guardianship), which is a rule on the end of guardianship and puberty, not a dedicated marriage clause; the draft's '14 for males' is a puberty figure, and Justinian's text does not state a 'marriage age of 14'. Institutes text does not mention betrothal at seven; the seven-year rule is Digest 23.1.14 (Modestinus), not Institutes 1.10. Digest 23.2.4 concerns the validity of a marriage with a girl under 12 (wife's legal status), not a prohibition as such. Sandars 1876 is public domain; the Latin is a modern critical text.

claim: (c) Prochiron (Basil I, c. 870-879): marriage ages (draft: 12 girls / 14 boys) - not confirmed; (e) civil ban on fourth marriages (Prochiron IV.25)
ref: Procheiros Nomos (Prochiron, c. 872): Title II (marriage; index entry 'γάμος ἔγγραφος II, 3'), cap. 1 (concordance: taken from Ecloga II, 1); Title VI cap. 1 (wills, minors); Title III (betrothal, cap. 2-3); Title IV cap. 25-27 (fourth marriage; interpolation thesis of Oikonomides)
quote_orig: Title VI, 1 (OCR of Brandileone-Puntoni 1895, read; the Title II text is NOT in the OCR): "ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ ἀνήλικοι, τουϊτέστιν οὗ μὴ ὄντες ἄῤῥενες ἐτῶν ιδ΄, αἱ δὲ ϑήλειαι ἐτῶν ιβ΄ καὶ εἰσελϑοῦσαι εἰς ιγ΄"
own_translation_en: Prochiron VI, 1 (my literal English, not a published translation): "Likewise the minors, namely those who are not males of 14 years, or females of 12 years and entering their 13th year, are forbidden to make dispositions." The rule is about wills (dispositions), not marriage.
edition: Prochiron legum, ed. F. Brandileone and V. Puntoni (Rome: Forzani, 1895), from Vatican gr. 845; Internet Archive copy (Google scan), public domain (1895). Oikonomides (DOP 30, 1976) cites Freshfield's English of IV.26-27 as 'A Manual of Eastern Roman Law. The Procheiros Nomos (Cambridge, 1927)', while the draft says 1928: check the title page.
what_it_says: The draft's Prochiron marriage ages (12 girls / 14 boys) are NOT confirmed. The only Prochiron ages I could read are the minors' limits for making wills in Title VI (males under 14, females under 12). Brandileone's 1895 source-concordance (index 'Fonti') lists Prochiron Title II, cap. 1 as taken from Ecloga II, 1, which is the Ecloga's 15/13 marriage rule. This suggests the Prochiron's own marriage age is 15/13, not 12/14. This is an inference from the concordance and is NOT verified against the Greek text of Title II. Within Title III (betrothal) I could read no marriage-age clause.
limits: Prochiron Title II (marriage) and Title I are not present in the OCR text I downloaded (the scan text starts with the preface, then Title III cap. 2 at about p. 4). So the marriage clause itself was not read. The concordance is an editor's table (1895) and needs the page image or the Greek text to confirm. Milas (S3-04) says the Ecloga's 15/13 was later changed to 14/12 by later legal provisions, which he does not name in the note. Action for the orchestrator: check Brandileone-Puntoni 1895, Title II cap. 1 (page image on archive.org item prochironlegump01empigoog).

claim: (d) Nicodim Milas, Orthodox Church Law, §181: church law required an age sufficient for marriage (draft); also (b) Ecloga ages
ref: Nikodim Milaš (Nicodim Milas), Orthodox Church Law, § 181 'The Principal Conditions of Marriage', section 2 'The prescribed age for marriage', with notes [2]-[4]
quote_orig: Milas's own English text is the source; the notes contain Greek only in note [13] (not relevant to ages).
quote_en: "Both Roman and church legislation require that both the male and female must have reached mature age (ἥβη, pubertas) if they wish to contract a lawful marriage. Roman law, after various fluctuations on this question, established that a young man must be 14 years old and a girl 12 years old, when they wish to marry. The Church adopted these years for marriage, and made them law through several synodal decisions."  Note [2] (English, quoted): "In the Ekloga (II, 1; cf. the Kormchaia, ch. 49, section 2, 1) it was prescribed that a bridegroom be 15 years and a girl 13, but this was changed by the legal provisions just mentioned."
edition: Orthodox Church Law by Saint Nikodim Milaš, English text on Royal Archives site (royalarchives.org). The page does NOT state the translator, the original publication date or the translation date; I did not verify them. Not checked for licence: treat as a web reproduction.
what_it_says: Milas states that Roman law fixed marriage age at 14 for a young man and 12 for a girl, that the Church adopted these ages through synodal decisions, and that the Ecloga had 15 and 13 but that this was changed. He cites Prochiron IV, 2 among sources for the 14/12 rule. Milas does not say that the Church approved child marriage; he says 'mature age' (pubertas) was required.
limits: (1) The draft's wording 'required an age sufficient for marriage' is imprecise: Milas gives specific ages 14/12. (2) His citation of 'Prochiron IV, 2' for these ages does not match the text I read: Prochiron Title IV (on dowry) chapters 1 and beginning of 2 concern dowry, with no marriage age in them (OCR of 1895 edition, see S3-03). (3) Milas's note [4] says modern civil codes differed (e.g. Hungary 18/16). (4) His statement that the Ecloga had 15/13 supports the Fordham excerpt (S3-01). (5) Milas's text is a modern English rendering; I could not confirm which translation or edition.

claim: (e) Basil of Caesarea canon 4: penances for second to fourth marriages (draft: canons 4 and 50 on second to fourth marriages)
ref: Basil of Caesarea, First Canonical Epistle to Amphilochius (Letter 188, 'Canonica Prima'), Canon IV
url: https://biblehub.com/library/schaff/the_seven_ecumenical_councils/v_the_first_canonical_epistle.htm (Schaff translation; the same canonical letter is in NPNF2 vol. 8 as Letter CLXXXVIII)
quote_orig: Greek not obtained (the Greek original was not opened)
quote_en: "They that marry a second time, used to be under penance a year or two. They that marry a third time, three or four years. But we have a custom, that he who marries a third time be under penance five years, not by canon, but tradition."
edition: Translation by Philip Schaff, The Seven Ecumenical Councils (NPNF2 vol. 14, 1900), public domain; text read on Biblehub. Also in NPNF2 vol. 8 (1895).
what_it_says: Basil's canon 4 sets penances for second marriages (one to two years) and third marriages (three to four years) and notes a local custom of five years for a third marriage, 'not by canon'. It does not mention a fourth marriage and gives no ban on a fourth.
limits: Basil's canon 4 is not a ban on a third marriage at all; the draft's 'canons 4 and 50 on second to fourth marriages' overstates it. The fourth-marriage prohibition is not in canon 4. Canon 50 (see S3-06) says there is no law on trigamy.

claim: (e) Basil canons 50 and 80: rules on third and fourth marriages; (f) whether a later marriage with a living first wife is void
ref: Basil of Caesarea, Canonical Letter 199 ('Canonica Secunda'), canon L (=50); and canon LXXX (printed after Letter CC in NPNF2 vol. 8)
url: https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf208.all.html (NPNF2 vol. 8, full volume, Schaff ed.; canon L text at the Letter CXCIX section)
quote_en: Canon L (=50): "There is no law as to trigamy: a third marriage is not contracted by law. We look upon such things as the defilements of the Church. But we do not subject them to public condemnation, as being better than unrestrained fornication."  Canon LXXX (=80): "On polygamy the Fathers are silent, as being brutish and altogether inhuman. The sin seems to me worse than fornication."
edition: NPNF2 vol. 8 (Basil: Letters and Select Works), Philip Schaff ed., 1895, public domain; text read on CCEL. The note under canon LXXX (editors/Benedictine annotator and the Dictionary of Christian Antiquities, vol. ii, p. 1104) is secondary.
what_it_says: Canon 50 says canon law has no rule on a third marriage and that Basil does not impose public condemnation on it. Canon 80 treats polygamy as worse than fornication, and the NPNF editorial note reports that Zonaras and Balsamon read 'polygamy' as a fourth marriage, with trigamy 'permitted though discouraged'.
limits: (1) Canon 50 is the strongest evidence that third marriages were not forbidden by canon law in Basil's time; the draft's implicit view (canon law 'forbade' 3rd/4th marriages) must be qualified. (2) The 'Zonaras and Balsamon' reading is secondary (an editorial note, not Balsamon's text, which I did not read). (3) Canon 80's wording on 'polygamy' is an editorial translation issue, as the note itself says. (4) No passage in these canons addresses a marriage contracted while a first wife lives (see S3-08).

claim: (e) Tomos of Union (920): ban on fourth marriages and limits on third ones
ref: John Meyendorff, 'Christian Marriage in Byzantium: The Canonical and Liturgical Tradition', Dumbarton Oaks Papers 44 (1990), p. 102 (section on successive marriages; cf. Canon 4, RPS IV p. 102 in his notes)
url: https://archive.org/details/DOP44_07_Meyendorff (full text read: https://archive.org/download/DOP44_07_Meyendorff/DOP44_07_Meyendorff_djvu.txt). Item in the Dumbarton Oaks Papers collection; no access restriction in metadata; licence status not confirmed
quote_en: "Totally forbidding a fourth marriage, the Tome also places strict limitations on a third" (first 16 words of a longer passage; the full passage is about 90 words and is not reproduced).
edition: DOP 44 (1990), Dumbarton Oaks copyright; short quote only. Meyendorff's account is secondary; the Greek text of the Tome (Rhalles-Potles VI) was not read.
what_it_says: The Tome of Union of 920 is described by Meyendorff as the 'most solemn set of rules' on successive marriages; it totally forbids a fourth marriage and limits a third (penance of five years at age 40+ with no children from a previous marriage; four years at age 30). The Tome is thus a 920 Constantinopolitan settlement, not a canon of Basil.
limits: Secondary account (Meyendorff 1990) plus the NPNF editorial note's summary from the Dictionary of Christian Antiquities (vol. ii, p. 1104), which says the 920 council set excommunication for a fourth marriage and, for a third at age forty, suspension for five years. I did not read the Greek Tome.

claim: (e) Fourth marriage ban in Byzantine civil law (Leo VI, Novel 90; Procheiros IV.25) and (f) whether a marriage contracted while the first wife was alive was void
ref: Nicolas Oikonomides, 'Leo VI's Legislation of 907 Forbidding Fourth Marriages: An Interpolation in the Procheiros Nomos (IV, 25-27)', Dumbarton Oaks Papers 30 (1976), pp. 175 (intro), 181-186 (civil legislation; Novel 90 p. 183; Procheiros IV p. 185-186)
url: https://archive.org/details/DOP30_08_Oikonomides (full text read: https://archive.org/download/DOP30_08_Oikonomides/DOP30_08_Oikonomides_djvu.txt); Dumbarton Oaks Papers collection; licence not confirmed
quote_orig: Greek of Novel 90 and Procheiros IV.25-27 as printed by Oikonomides (not reproduced here; the Greek was read in the article footnote and text)
quote_en: Intro, p. 175: "they never mentioned a fourth marriage expressis verbis".  Civil legislation, p. 181-182 (Isaurian Ecloga): "contains no provisions concerning third or fourth marriages".  Novel 90, p. 183-184: Leo "legalizes" the penance for third marriages but "contests neither the validity of the third marriage once celebrated, nor the legitimacy of the children".
own_translation_en: Procheiros IV.25 (Oikonomides' summary, p. 185): the 'ancient' law confirmed by Justinian allowed cohabitation up to a fourth marriage; the paragraph forbidding a fourth marriage is, in Oikonomides' view, a 907 addition (interpolation). Freshfield's English of IV.26-27 is cited by Oikonomides as 'Cambridge 1927', the draft says 1928.
edition: DOP 30 (1976), Dumbarton Oaks. Copyright is held by the publisher; quotes above are short (<=40 words). Oikonomides' own argument (interpolation of 907) is a scholarly hypothesis, not a settled fact.
what_it_says: Oikonomides argues: canon law never explicitly named a fourth marriage; the Ecloga (726) has no rule on third or fourth marriages; Leo VI's Novel 90 (before 899) condemns third marriages but does not void them; the explicit fourth-marriage ban in Procheiros IV.25-27 is, on his argument, a later interpolation from 907. Civil law therefore did not clearly forbid a fourth marriage before 907.
limits: Oikonomides' interpolation thesis is contested or at least a hypothesis, and the article is 1976. I did not verify the Greek of Novel 90 against the Zepos text. He says Novel 90 'contests neither the validity of the third marriage' - this is the opposite of the 'first wife' loophole logic for later marriages. Nothing in this article addresses marriage while a first wife was alive, so (f) remains unverified here.

claim: (a)/(d) Church and Byzantine minimum ages (14/12) and Milutin's marriage to Simonis (1299, aged about five)
ref: John Meyendorff, DOP 44 (1990), p. 103 (section on minimum age and on Milutin), with note 24 (citing M. Lascaris, Vizantiske princeze, 1926, p. 58)
quote_en: "The minimum age for marriage was fixed by Justinian's Code to fourteen for men and twelve for women, but diplomatic requirements sometimes made this rule flexible."  And: "the Serbian Kral' Milutin married Simonis, daughter of Emperor Andronicus II, when she was only five (1299)."
edition: DOP 44 (1990), Dumbarton Oaks copyright; short quotes only.
what_it_says: Meyendorff gives the Justinianic minimum ages as 14 for men and 12 for women, and says diplomatic needs made the rule flexible. He cites the Milutin-Simonis marriage of 1299 when she was five as a well-known example, citing Lascaris 1926.
limits: Meyendorff gives age 5 for 1299; the draft's 'five or six' is a hedged version of the same figure and is not contradicted. The Greek of the Justinianic texts was not read here (see S3-02). Meyendorff does not discuss the Ecloga or Milas.

claim: (f) 'First wife' loophole: whether canon law treated a marriage contracted while a previous wife was alive as no marriage (bigamy)
ref: Negative result: no primary or scholarly statement on this point found in the sources I opened (Basil canons IV, L, LXXX; Oikonomides 1976; Meyendorff 1990; Milas §181)
what_it_says: I could not verify from primary or accessible scholarly sources that Byzantine canon law declared a later marriage void because an earlier wife was alive. Basil's canon 50 says there is no law on trigamy; Meyendorff and Oikonomides discuss third and fourth marriages, not the living-spouse question.
limits: Fine (1987) was not opened (no legitimate open copy found). The 'first wife was alive, so marriages two and three were not marriages' argument appears only in the draft's quotation of Fine p. 222; I have not verified it, and the canons and secondary works I read say nothing on it.

claim: (b) Ecloga of Leo III and Constantine V (726), Title II: minimum ages (draft: 13 girls, 15 boys); whether the Ecloga says anything about consummation before the age
ref: Ecloga Leonis et Constantini, Title II (ΤΙΤΛΟΣ ΔΕΥΤΕΡΟΣ, 'Περὶ γάμων ἐπιτετραμμένων καὶ κεκωλυμένων'), chapter 1 (α'), Greek text with variants, ed. K. E. Zachariae a Lingenthal
quote_orig: "Συνίσταται γάμος Χριστιανῶν, εἴτε ἐγγράφως εἴτε ἀγράφως, μεταξὺ ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ... τοῦ μὲν ἀνδρὸς ἀπὸ ιε ἔτους χρόνου, τῆς δὲ γυναικὸς ἀπὸ ιγ ἔτους χρόνου, ἀμφοτέρων θελόντων μετὰ τῆς τῶν γονέων συναινέσεως."  (ιε = 15, ιγ = 13 in Greek numerals; read from the 1852 print via OCR, numerals clear)
quote_en: "A Christian marriage is contracted, whether in writing or unwritten, between a man and a woman ... for the man from the 15th year of age, for the woman from the 13th year, both wishing it, with the consent of their parents."  (my own literal English of the Greek; the Freshfield English is in S3-01)
own_translation_en: Literal English of the Greek chapter, as above (my translation, not published).
edition: Ecloga Leonis et Constantini, ed. K. E. Zachariae a Lingenthal, in Collectio librorum juris Graeco-Romani ineditorum (Leipzig, 1852), pub. 1852; public domain. Scanned on Internet Archive.
what_it_says: The Ecloga's Title II, chapter 1, fixes the minimum age of marriage at 15 for a man and 13 for a woman, and requires parental consent. This matches the Fordham excerpt (S3-01) and the draft (13 girls / 15 boys). The Greek reading gives no other age, and no clause on consummation in Title II: a keyword search for 'puberty', 'consummation' and similar terms in Title II found nothing relevant.
limits: The Greek edition is a 19th-century critical text (1852) with variants; the numeral reading comes from OCR and the numerals look clear. The Greek shown is normalised (accents and the OCR spelling of 'ἔτους' corrected). The keyword search for consummation is not exhaustive; I did not read every line, but no consummation-age rule appears in Title II. The Ecloga (726) is about 570 years before the 1299 marriage; Milas says the 15/13 ages were later changed to 14/12 (S3-04).
